---
title: "Making coding agents dependable"
date: "2026-08-25"
description: "Four assumptions I changed after building tools for context measurement, compression, and API access."
format: article
theme: "AI-enabled engineering"
---

The broad coding-agent infrastructure checklist is no longer especially interesting. Durable task state, context engineering, sandbox policy, tool permissions, trace evaluation, and post-PR automation are all documented and, in several products, shipping. OpenAI has written about the [agent harness](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/), Anthropic about [evaluating trajectories and outcomes](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents), and the MCP maintainers about why [tool annotations are hints rather than enforcement](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-03-16-tool-annotations/). A recent book-length treatment even frames reliable agents around an [evidence chain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13867).

I don't have another checklist to add. I have four narrower lessons from building tools around coding agents. In each case, something could be technically correct while still giving a false sense of completeness.

## A balanced number can still hide most of the system

I built [peek](https://github.com/mstuart/peek) to inspect historical Claude Code and Codex sessions. I initially thought Codex logs exposed enough information to produce a near-exact account of context composition.

The first real capture refuted that. Codex reported 37,476 input tokens. After counting the visible base instructions and dynamic tool definitions, 25,265 tokens were still unexplained: a 67.4% residual.

The accounting equation balanced, but most of the input was not explained. Those are different claims.

That distinction now matters to me more than the chart. An agent system should label what was measured, estimated, inferred, or refuted. An unknown remainder should stay unknown. Otherwise observability becomes a way to make guesses look authoritative.

The same applies to task state. Repository instructions, a user's request, an agent's assumption, a prior-run memory, and a live check may all appear in one context window. They should not become the same kind of fact merely because they are represented as text.

## Fewer input tokens can be the wrong optimization

I built [tare](https://github.com/mstuart/tare) to reduce the context occupied by tool output, logs, JSON, file reads, and history. On its committed `agent_context` corpus, `tare compress` reduced 15,130 tokens to 8,499, or 43.8%.

That result proves a bounded thing: the transform made that corpus smaller. It does not prove that an agent completed tasks more reliably, cost less overall, or preserved every detail it later needed.

Input size is only one part of the bill. Rewriting a stable cached prefix can forfeit a provider's cache discount. Compressing too aggressively can also make the model spend more output tokens reconstructing what was removed. Tare leaves an explicitly cached prefix alone and treats an output spike as a reason to back off, but I have not published a repeated task-success study showing that this controller improves outcomes.

The useful target is not the smallest prompt. It is the lowest total cost that preserves the task: input, cache writes and reads, output, latency, and success. A smaller context can be a worse context.

## A valid call can still be the wrong action

[graphql-agent-toolkit](https://github.com/mstuart/graphql-agent-toolkit) generates typed operations and agent tools from a GraphQL schema. Building it reinforced a boundary that type systems cannot cross: a schema can describe how to call an operation, but not whether the caller should.

A mutation can be valid against the schema and still exceed what the user delegated. It can be safe for one set of arguments and destructive for another. It can succeed with credentials broader than the task required.

MCP already defines read-only, destructive, idempotent, and open-world hints. The maintainers are explicit that these annotations are untrusted metadata. The decision still has to be made at invocation time from the exact arguments, credentials, current state, and approval that authorized the work.

Type-safe is not policy-safe. A successful tool result should therefore carry evidence another step can check, not just a success-shaped string.

## Green is a property of evidence, not of a task

The first real `peek bench` comparison ran one task under two Claude Code configurations. Both passed the supplied verifier. One used 19.1% fewer tokens and cost 93.4% less, with 1.1 seconds more wall time.

The honest conclusion is that both configurations passed one verifier once, in that environment, and one run was cheaper. It is not that the cheaper configuration is generally better or more dependable. That would require repeated trials, audited graders, pinned environments, and more representative tasks.

I now read every green result this way. A test pass belongs to a revision, verifier, environment, and time. Review, rebases, deployment, and production traffic can each make earlier evidence stale. "The task passed" throws away the information needed to decide whether it still has.

This is the thread connecting the three tools. A reconciled token count, a smaller context, a valid operation, and a green test can all be correct and insufficient. Making coding agents dependable starts with refusing to launder partial evidence into certainty.

I don't yet have evidence that this is enough. I do have evidence that systems become hard to trust when they blur what they observed, what they inferred, what they were allowed to do, and what remains unknown.
